summary.title: 8.1.1.1. (NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods: Assessing Product Reliability)
summary.one_liner: Reliability is quality over time: it measures how units keep meeting specifications during operation, not just at the start of life, and is modeled with life distributions.
takeaways: Quality is a snapshot at the start of use; reliability is a motion picture of day-by-day operation.
Time zero defects are manufacturing mistakes that escaped final test; later failures are reliability defects or fallout.
Reliability fallout is described with a life distribution model giving the fraction failing over time.
summary.summary: This short section of the NIST/SEMATECH Engineering Statistics Handbook introduces why product reliability matters. It defines quality as conformance to requirements at the start of use, measured by the fraction of shipped units meeting specifications. It then contrasts this snapshot with reliability, which tracks how units keep meeting specifications over time, such as after a week, a month, or a warranty period. The page notes that the fraction of failures over time is described by a life distribution model.
